name: Chepang
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 9 other works read were silent
catalog_quote: Stress is non-contrastive and occurs on the first of a sequence of combined syllables - that is, word initially.
sweep_summary: Chepang (chep1245) is in the catalog as fixed-strict (word-initial) on Caughley 1982 PL B-84 p. 39. this search of works with stress in the title had one title hit, Pittman 1970 'Gurung, Tamang, Thakali, Sherpa, and Chepang prosodies' (Hale & Pike eds., Wolfenden OP 3:2, pp. 1-8).org: the full Part II scan (micro_IA41153125_0127) is open on archive.org and was downloaded (24 MB, 136 pp, with scanned text); the chapter (scan pp. 7-14) was extracted and its pages 2, 6, 7 checked against the images. It is a comparative register paper: for Chepang it reports only a two-way high/low pitch class on monosyllabic word-bases predictable from final-consonant voicing (p. 2, p. 6 section 11); 'stress' is used only of Tamang. It is silent on Chepang word-stress placement, so the catalog's classification stands. A bonus open source was also downloaded (Caughley & Caughley 1970 Chepang Texts, Appendix A p. 124, Part IV, via the Rosetta Project extract): 'Tone: As analyzed it is not phonemic.. most apparent when the syllable is initial in a phonological word' - also silent on stress position. The best first-hand statement remains Pons 2022 section 2.10.2 pp. 209-210 (held from the 9/16 check, re-read today): stress on the first syllable at word level, main cue F0, confirming the classification and superseding the one-line 1982 source in strength of the evidence. Nothing left to acquire for this language from this search of works with stress in the title; written at

new_statements.quote: Monosyllabic, dissyllabic or trisyllabic roots or stems can form a word that in all cases, except for determinative or descriptive compound type 2, bears stress on the first syllable. Stress consistently applies at the word level, whether the word is pronounced in isolation, in a carrier phrase, or in a phrase in connected speech or natural discourse in absence of specific pragmatic intonation. In Chepang, the main acoustic cue for stress is pitch (F0). While intensity (or amplitude) often correlates with stress, it remains marginal, pitch being the most prominent feature.

new_statements.reading: Word stress is fixed on the first syllable of the word at the word level, cued mainly by F0; the only exception named is one compound type. Confirms the catalog's fixed-strict word-initial coding. Caveat on 'new': this file was downloaded and read by the 9/16 check stage (recorded there as 'confirms', action upgrade-evidence-grade); I re-read the passage first-hand today. sources.quote: "3. Tone: As analyzed it is not phonemic. Syllables ending in a voiceless consonant are, however, higher in pitch than other syllables; this effect is most apparent when the syllable is initial in a phonological word."
sources.note: Earliest Caughley statement on Chepang suprasegmentals: tone non-phonemic, pitch raised by voiceless finals, most visibly in word-initial syllables. No mention of stress or its position; silent on the catalog's classification, consistent with the 1982 grammar.

sources.quote: p. 6, section 11: "Chepang, instead of four possible prosodic patterns for each monosyllabic word-base allows only two: high or low. These, as indicated earlier, are correlated with final voicing: all highs have voiceless finals and vice versa; all lows have voiced finals and vice versa. Final glottal stop and final h both pattern with the highs." p. 2: "Ross and Kathleen Caughley, Ballabh Mani Dahal, and Chuda Mani Bandhu, working on Chepang ... found, in the spring of 1969, that every consonant except s and h occurs both voiced and voiceless, and that all words with final voiceless consonants are high pitch, whereas those with final voiced consonants are low."
sources.locator: p. 2 (section 4, Table 4) and pp. 6-7 (section 11, Table 12); scan PDF pp. 8 and 12-13; pages verified against the page images
sources.note: A comparative register paper (the K/G 'tense/lax' hypothesis across Gurung, Tamang, Thakali, Sherpa, Chepang). For Chepang it only reports a two-way high/low pitch class on monosyllabic word-bases that is predictable from final-consonant voicing (taken from Caughley's then-unpublished phonemic summary, fn. 1). The word 'stress' occurs only for Tamang word-bases ('high stressed', 'mid stressed', 'low stressed', 'unstressed', pp. 2-3) and in the general list of possible exponents of the register contrast ('pitch, voice quality and stress', p. 8).
